title: Cancel the Fewest Meetings So That None Clash

concept.title: Keep the meeting that ends first, then the next one that starts after it, and so on
body: You are given `n` meetings, each from `s` to `e`. Two meetings **clash** when they share some time (a meeting that starts at the moment another ends is fine). What is the **smallest number of meetings you must cancel** so that no two of the remaining meetings clash? For `1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 1-3` the answer is 1: cancel `1-3`.

Cancelling the fewest is the same as **keeping the most**. This is the classic *activity selection* problem. Sort the meetings by their **end time**. Always keep the meeting that ends the earliest, because it leaves the largest part of the timeline free for the others. Then skip every meeting that starts before this one ends, and keep the next one that starts at or after it. Repeat.

body.code:
meetings.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])       # by the end time
kept = 0
last_end = -1
for s, e in meetings:
    if s >= last_end:                  # no clash with the last kept meeting
        kept += 1
        last_end = e
print(n - kept)

body: Why is "the earliest end" safe? Take any best schedule and look at its first meeting. Replacing it by the meeting with the earliest end time cannot create a clash, since the new meeting finishes no later, so a best schedule that starts with the earliest-ending meeting exists. The same argument applies to the rest of the schedule. The cost is the sort: O(n log n).

statement: `n` meetings are given by their start `s` and end `e`. Two meetings clash if they have some common time; a meeting that starts when another ends does not clash with it. Print the smallest number of meetings to cancel so that the remaining ones do not clash.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of meetings.
Each of the next `n` lines has two numbers `s` and `e`: the meeting occupies the time from `s` up to `e`.
outputFormat: Print the smallest number of meetings to cancel.
constraints: Two meetings clash if they share some time; a meeting may start exactly when another one ends.

examples.note: Only one of the three can stay: 2.

hints: Cancelling the fewest means keeping the most.
Sort the meetings by the end time.
Keep a meeting when its start is not before the end of the last kept one.

import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
meetings = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

explanation: The meetings are sorted by end time; each meeting whose start is not before the end of the last kept meeting is kept. The answer is n minus the number of kept meetings.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
meetings = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

meetings.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])
kept = 0
last_end = -1
for s, e in meetings:
    if s >= last_end:
        kept += 1
        last_end = e
print(n - kept)
